title: Laboratory Work and Industrial Chemistry
lines: Practical questions test judgement: is this operation safe, is this apparatus right, does this method really separate or identify the substance? Industrial questions apply equilibrium and rate ideas to real plants. Read every option slowly, because one wrong word ("dilute" for "concentrated") makes it false.
## Lab safety
- Dilute concentrated H₂SO₄ by pouring the acid slowly into water while stirring, never water into acid (the heat makes water boil and spit).

- Acid on skin: rinse with plenty of water, then apply dilute NaHCO₃ solution. Alkali on skin: rinse with water, then dilute boric acid. Acid in eyes: rinse with water while blinking, never rub, see a doctor.
- Spilled burning alcohol or small fires on the bench: cover with a damp cloth or sand. Burning sodium or magnesium: sand only, never water or CO₂ extinguishers.

- Never light a flammable gas (H₂, CH₄, CO) before testing its purity, or it may explode. Heat a test tube evenly first, point its mouth away from people, and keep the solid-heating tube's mouth slightly lower so condensed water does not crack it.
- Toxic gases (Cl₂, SO₂, NO₂, H₂S) are made in a fume cupboard and their tail gas absorbed (NaOH solution for Cl₂, SO₂, NO₂). CO is burned or collected in a balloon.
- Sodium and potassium are stored under kerosene; white phosphorus under water; concentrated HNO₃ and AgNO₃ in brown bottles; NaOH solution in bottles with rubber stoppers.
- Safety symbols: corrosive (H₂SO₄, NaOH), flammable (ethanol), toxic (CO), explosive.
! Trap: when stopping a heated reaction that collects gas over water, take the delivery tube out of the water first, then remove the flame; otherwise water sucks back into the hot tube.
## Common apparatus
- Heated directly: test tube, evaporating dish, crucible. Heated on gauze: beaker, flask, conical flask. Never heated: measuring cylinder, volumetric flask, reagent bottle.

- Measuring: measuring cylinder (to 0.1 mL), burette and pipette (to 0.01 mL), balance (to 0.1 g on a school top-pan balance). A volumetric flask makes a solution of exact concentration at one volume only.

- Separation: funnel (filtration), separating funnel (extraction, separating immiscible liquids), distillation flask with thermometer bulb at the side-arm, Liebig condenser with cooling water entering at the bottom and leaving at the top.

- Making a solution of known concentration: calculate, weigh, dissolve in a beaker, cool, transfer with rinsing (two or three times) into the volumetric flask, add water until 1–2 cm below the mark, then use a dropper to the mark, invert to mix.
> Example: When making 250 mL of 0.1 mol/L NaCl, a student looks up at the mark while topping up. Is the concentration high or low?
> Looking up makes the liquid seem lower, so the student adds too much water. The volume is too large, so the concentration is low.
- Other errors: not rinsing the beaker loses solute (low); transferring a hot solution, then cooling, leaves a smaller volume (high); water already in the flask has no effect.
## Preparing and collecting gases

- Choose the generator from the reactant states: solid + solid with heat (test tube, mouth slightly down); solid + liquid without heat (flask or test tube with a funnel); solid or liquid + liquid with heat (round-bottom flask on gauze).

- Choose collection by solubility and density (compare M with 29 for air): over water for gases insoluble in water; upward air displacement (open end up, gas in at the bottom) for gases denser than air; downward air displacement for gases lighter than air.
- O₂: 2KMnO₄ → K₂MnO₄ + MnO₂ + O₂↑ (heat); 2KClO₃ → 2KCl + 3O₂↑ (MnO₂, heat); 2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂↑ (MnO₂, no heat). Collect over water or upward air displacement. Test: relights a glowing splint.
- H₂: Zn + H₂SO₄(dilute) → ZnSO₄ + H₂↑. Collect over water or downward air displacement. Test: burns with a squeaky pop.

- CO₂: CaCO₃ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂↑. Collect by upward air displacement (it dissolves somewhat in water). Test: limewater turns cloudy. Do not use H₂SO₄ (CaSO₄ coats the marble and stops the reaction).

- NH₃: 2NH₄Cl + Ca(OH)₂ → CaCl₂ + 2NH₃↑ + 2H₂O (heat, solid + solid). Dry with soda lime or CaO, never with concentrated H₂SO₄ or CaCl₂. Collect by downward air displacement; test with moist red litmus (turns blue) or a glass rod dipped in concentrated HCl (white smoke).

- Cl₂: MnO₂ + 4HCl(conc.) → MnCl₂ + Cl₂↑ + 2H₂O (heat). Pass through saturated NaCl solution (removes HCl), then concentrated H₂SO₄ (removes water). Collect by upward air displacement or over saturated NaCl solution; absorb excess with NaOH. Test: moist starch-KI paper turns blue.
> Example: Which pair of gases can both be dried with concentrated H₂SO₄ and collected by upward air displacement: (A) NH₃, O₂ (B) Cl₂, CO₂ (C) H₂, SO₂ (D) HCl, H₂S?
> NH₃ reacts with H₂SO₄; H₂ is lighter than air; H₂S is oxidised by concentrated H₂SO₄. Cl₂ (M = 71) and CO₂ (M = 44) are acidic or neutral, not reducing, and denser than air. B is correct.
! Order rule: wash gases through solutions first and dry last, otherwise the gas picks up water again.
## Separation and purification

- Filtration separates an insoluble solid from a liquid. "One sticks, two lower, three touches": paper sticks to the funnel, paper below the funnel rim, liquid below the paper rim, and the glass rod, beaker spout and funnel tip touch where they should.

- Evaporation and crystallisation: evaporate to obtain a solute whose solubility changes little with temperature (NaCl), stopping heating when most crystals have formed. Cooling crystallisation suits solutes whose solubility rises sharply with temperature (KNO₃); it also removes a little NaCl from KNO₃. Hydrated salts (CuSO₄·5H₂O) are obtained by evaporating, cooling and crystallising, not by evaporating to dryness.
- Distillation separates miscible liquids with different boiling points (ethanol from water, fresh water from sea water). Add boiling chips; thermometer bulb at the side-arm level.

- Extraction and separation: a solute moves from water into an immiscible solvent in which it dissolves better (I₂ from water into CCl₄ or benzene). CCl₄ is denser than water (lower layer); benzene is less dense (upper layer). Drain the lower layer through the tap and pour the upper layer from the top.

- Chemical purification: add a reagent that removes the impurity without adding a new one. CO₂ containing HCl: saturated NaHCO₃ solution. Cl₂ containing HCl: saturated NaCl solution. FeCl₂ containing FeCl₃: add iron powder and filter. FeCl₃ containing FeCl₂: pass Cl₂. Na₂CO₃ solid containing NaHCO₃: heat. CH₄ containing C₂H₄: bromine water.
> Example: Crude salt contains Ca²⁺, Mg²⁺ and SO₄²⁻. In what order do you add BaCl₂, NaOH, Na₂CO₃ and HCl?
> Na₂CO₃ must come after BaCl₂ so that it also removes the excess Ba²⁺. Then filter, and add HCl last to remove excess OH⁻ and CO₃²⁻. A valid order is BaCl₂, NaOH, Na₂CO₃, filter, HCl.
! Trap: ethanol cannot extract iodine from water because ethanol mixes with water.
## Identifying substances

- Use a reagent that gives a different observation for every substance. One reagent can tell apart many solutions if it gives distinct results: Ba(OH)₂ solution with warming distinguishes NH₄Cl (gas), Na₂SO₄ (white precipitate), (NH₄)₂SO₄ (gas and precipitate) and NaCl (no change).
- Gas tests: O₂ glowing splint; H₂ pop; CO₂ limewater; NH₃ red litmus; Cl₂ starch-KI paper; SO₂ decolourises magenta and the colour returns on heating.
- Water: anhydrous CuSO₄ turns from white to blue.
## Industrial processes

- Haber process: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃, ΔH < 0. Conditions: about 400–500 °C (a compromise: lower temperature gives more NH₃ but too slowly, and suits the iron catalyst's activity), 10–30 MPa (high pressure raises yield and rate), iron catalyst, NH₃ liquefied and removed, unreacted gases recycled.

- Contact process for sulfuric acid: S or FeS₂ burnt to SO₂ (4FeS₂ + 11O₂ → 2Fe₂O₃ + 8SO₂); 2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃, ΔH < 0, with V₂O₅ catalyst at about 400–500 °C and normal pressure (conversion is already high, so expensive high pressure is not worth it); SO₃ absorbed in 98 % concentrated H₂SO₄, not water, to avoid an acid mist.
- Nitric acid: 4NH₃ + 5O₂ → 4NO + 6H₂O (Pt); 2NO + O₂ → 2NO₂; 3NO₂ + H₂O → 2HNO₃ + NO.
- Chlor-alkali: electrolysis of brine with a cation-exchange membrane gives NaOH, Cl₂ and H₂.

- Metal extraction depends on activity: very active metals (K, Na, Mg, Al) by electrolysis of molten compounds; middle metals (Zn, Fe, Cu) by reduction with C, CO, H₂ or Al (blast furnace: Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂; limestone removes SiO₂ as slag CaSiO₃); inactive metals (Hg, Ag) by heating their oxides: 2HgO → 2Hg + O₂.
> Example: Why is the Haber process run at about 450 °C even though a lower temperature gives a higher equilibrium yield?
> At low temperature the rate is too slow and the catalyst is not active enough. About 450 °C balances an acceptable yield with a fast enough rate.
! Memory trick: "Exothermic equilibrium in industry is always a compromise temperature; pressure goes high only when it pays." Haber uses high pressure; the contact process does not.
